questions.question: A user has an eligible Microsoft 365 license but no Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on. What grounding does their Copilot Chat (Basic) experience use by default?
choices: No grounding at all; it answers only from the model's training data, with no web access
Web grounding only; it can't reach organizational data through Microsoft Graph
Microsoft Graph grounding across every site, mailbox and chat the user can open
Web grounding plus the user's own mailbox and OneDrive files, but not SharePoint sites
questions.explanation: Copilot Chat (Basic) is the baseline experience included with eligible Microsoft 365 licenses. It is web-grounded and can't use organizational data via Microsoft Graph. Work content gets in only when the user uploads or pastes it, uses Copilot Chat in Teams or Outlook on open content, or uses a pay-as-you-go agent that has access to org content. Coaching angle: 'free Copilot' is not the same as a Copilot that knows your business.

questions.question: Which three routes does Microsoft list for getting organizational content into a Copilot Chat (Basic) conversation?
choices: Semantic index search across SharePoint, Copilot connectors for line-of-business data, or a free SharePoint agent
Copilot Search on the web, Copilot Notebooks with linked files, or the Microsoft 365 Copilot mobile app's file picker
Microsoft Graph grounding in chat, the Researcher agent, or any declarative agent built in Agent Builder at no charge
Upload or paste it, use Copilot Chat in Teams or Outlook on open content, or use a PAYG agent with org access
questions.explanation: Basic users can't use Graph grounding. Microsoft lists three ways org content reaches them: upload or paste it with the prompt, use Copilot Chat in Teams or Outlook with the content open, or use a pay-as-you-go (metered) agent that has access to org content. That third route is where unexpected metered spend usually comes from.

questions.question: Microsoft's license comparison labels some users 'Microsoft 365 Copilot (Basic)'. What distinguishes them from 'Copilot Chat (Basic)' users?
choices: They're Copilot Business users, which Microsoft labels Basic in tenants with fewer than 300 seats
They have no Copilot add-on but still get standard access to Copilot in Word, Excel, PowerPoint and OneNote
They hold the Copilot add-on, but their tenant hasn't finished the Microsoft Graph semantic indexing that Premium needs
They signed in to Copilot with a personal Microsoft account rather than an Entra ID work account
questions.explanation: Neither label means a paid Copilot license. 'Copilot Chat (Basic)' users don't get Copilot in Word, Excel, PowerPoint and OneNote. 'Microsoft 365 Copilot (Basic)' users get standard access to Copilot in those apps but still no Graph grounding. 'Premium' means the paid Microsoft 365 Copilot license: full experience, priority access, and grounding in web, Graph and Work IQ.

questions.question: What does the Microsoft 365 Copilot (Premium) license add over the free Copilot Chat baseline, according to Microsoft's overview?
choices: Access to GPT and Claude models, which the free Copilot Chat tier doesn't offer at any level
Automatic grounding in web, Microsoft Graph and Work IQ, plus the full in-app experience
Unlimited Copilot Credits for Cowork, Code and Autopilot, with no usage-based billing at all
The ability to sign in with an Entra ID work account and get Enterprise Data Protection
questions.explanation: Premium is grounded in the web plus Microsoft Graph and Work IQ automatically, and adds the full in-app experience plus admin features such as Copilot Search, SharePoint Advanced Management and semantic indexing. It does not include unlimited usage of 'advanced AI' like Cowork. Those are metered in Copilot Credits.

questions.question: What protects Copilot Chat conversations for users who sign in with a Microsoft Entra work account, even without a paid Copilot license?
choices: Microsoft Purview Information Barriers
Restricted Content Discovery
Customer Lockbox for Copilot
Enterprise Data Protection (EDP)
questions.explanation: Copilot Chat signed in with an Entra ID account comes with Enterprise Data Protection, so prompts and responses get the commercial data protection terms. That is a useful point when a customer worries that staff are pasting data into consumer AI tools: the free, EDP-protected Copilot Chat is a safer default than shadow AI.

questions.question: How does Microsoft's Cowork admin documentation classify Copilot Cowork?
choices: As a Microsoft 365 Copilot feature that's fully included in the $30 seat, so admins govern it only through Teams app policies
As a declarative agent that runs entirely inside the $30 Copilot license with no metering
As a standalone Teams app that needs its own per-user add-on license from AppSource
As an agentic system rather than an agent, governed by usage-based billing spending policies
questions.explanation: Microsoft describes Cowork as an agentic system, different from an agent. It plans and runs long, multi-step tasks. It requires a Microsoft 365 Copilot license, and its usage (model responses, tool and skill calls, image generation, browser tasks) is billed in Copilot Credits through usage-based billing.

questions.question: An admin wants to stop a group of users from using Copilot Cowork. According to Microsoft's Cowork governance guidance, what actually blocks access?
choices: Unchecking Cowork under Agents > All Agents in the Microsoft 365 admin center
Setting a very low per-user credit limit, such as one credit, in their spending policy
Removing those users from every spending policy that includes Cowork
Turning off Cowork discovery so the entry point is hidden in the Copilot app for them
questions.explanation: Microsoft says a spending policy is an access control, not only a budget. Users get Cowork only through a policy whose scope includes them and that selects Cowork. A low credit limit doesn't block access, discovery settings only control visibility, and the old All Agents entry has no effect on who can use Cowork. To block, remove the users from every policy that includes Cowork.

questions.question: An admin creates a spending policy scoped to 'All users' with a 1-credit limit that selects Cowork, intending it as a placeholder. What is the effect?
choices: Nobody can use Cowork, since a one-credit limit is below the minimum size of any task
Cowork stays disabled until a P3 pre-purchase plan is attached to the spending policy
The whole tenant gets Cowork access; the policy grants access however small the limit
Only Global Administrators can use Cowork until the policy's limit is raised above one
questions.explanation: Microsoft's Cowork access page gives exactly this example: an 'All users' policy that selects Cowork grants the whole tenant access, even with a tiny limit. Policies are access grants first. Coaching angle: design spending policies around security groups, not 'All users', and review them like any other access grant.

questions.question: As of Ignite 2026, what is Autopilot in Microsoft 365 Copilot?
choices: A Copilot Studio setting that automatically publishes every new agent to all channels
A persistent personal agent with its own Entra Agent ID and a named manager (Frontier)
An Intune policy that silently deploys Copilot apps to unmanaged personal devices
The model router that picks between fast and reasoning models in Copilot Chat sessions
questions.explanation: Autopilot is a persistent agent that acts on a user's behalf, with its own agent identity and a named human manager. At Ignite 2026 it was Frontier-only and rolling out. Its agent account carries a recurring charge of 100 Copilot Credits per agent per month plus usage. The model router is a separate feature called Auto.

questions.question: Copilot Studio documentation now talks about 'harnesses'. Which statement matches Microsoft's description?
choices: The standard harness is Copilot Studio's established runtime; Copilot-harness agents bill differently
The standard harness is reserved for Dynamics 365 agents, and its usage is always free of charge
The standard harness is an older runtime Microsoft retired at Ignite 2026, and all agents now bill under one shared rate table
Every harness bills at the same per-message rate; the choice changes features, not cost
questions.explanation: Copilot Studio's billing and licensing pages are scoped to the 'standard harness'. Microsoft lists other harnesses, such as the Microsoft Copilot harness, the GitHub Copilot harness and the customer conversation harness, and says agents powered by the Microsoft Copilot harness are billed differently. When you see a credit rate table, check which harness it applies to.

questions.question: What did Microsoft announce as generally available at Ignite 2026 for hosting apps and agents built with Copilot Code, Cowork and Copilot Studio?
choices: Copilot Managed Runtime
Power Pages Agent Host
Microsoft Agent Grid
Azure Container Apps for Copilot
questions.explanation: Copilot Managed Runtime reached GA at Ignite 2026 as the hosting layer for apps and agents created in Code, Cowork and Copilot Studio. It is metered: Microsoft's credit guidance lists the Managed Runtime among usage-based services, with per-app monthly estimates ranging from tens to thousands of credits.

questions.question: Which statement about Work IQ APIs is correct according to Microsoft's Copilot Credits licensing guidance?
choices: Work IQ APIs are included in Microsoft 365 E5 and E7, but not in E3 or Business plans
Work IQ APIs aren't included as entitlements in the Microsoft 365 Copilot license and consume Copilot Credits
Work IQ APIs are part of every Microsoft 365 Copilot license, so external agents calling them for licensed users cost nothing extra
Work IQ APIs are billed per Entra Agent ID per month rather than per call or per task
questions.explanation: Microsoft's guidance is explicit that Work IQ APIs are not included as entitlements in the Microsoft Copilot license. Calls are metered in Copilot Credits, including when made from agents on other platforms such as Foundry. If a customer plans to have external agents pull Microsoft 365 context through Work IQ, budget for it.

questions.question: What is the defining difference between a declarative agent and a custom engine agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot?
choices: Declarative agents need Azure hosting at extra cost; custom engine agents need no extra hosting
Declarative agents must be written in code; custom engine agents can only be built in Agent Builder
Declarative agents use Copilot's own orchestrator and models; custom engine agents bring their own orchestrator and models
Declarative agents are defined in JSON and run only in Teams, while custom engine agents are defined in YAML and run only in Copilot Chat
questions.explanation: Declarative agents customize Copilot with instructions, knowledge and actions, but run on Copilot's orchestrator and foundation models with no extra hosting. Custom engine agents bring their own orchestrator and models and usually need hosting outside Microsoft 365, such as Azure, at additional cost.

questions.question: A customer wants an agent that proactively messages users and runs outside Microsoft 365 too. Per Microsoft's guidance, which agent type fits?
choices: A declarative agent built in Agent Builder
A SharePoint agent
A Copilot Chat agent grounded on public websites
A custom engine agent
questions.explanation: Microsoft's comparison says to build a custom engine agent when you need custom orchestration, your own models, proactive messaging, group use or use outside Microsoft 365. Declarative agents can't send proactive messages and live inside Copilot's experience.

questions.question: Who is responsible for compliance and responsible AI controls on a custom engine agent, compared with a declarative agent?
choices: The builder handles them for a custom engine agent; a declarative agent inherits Microsoft 365's
Microsoft owns compliance for both types, because any agent that appears in Microsoft 365 is covered by the same Product Terms
Neither has any compliance controls until the tenant licenses Agent 365 for its makers
The builder must supply content filters for a declarative agent but not a custom engine one
questions.explanation: Because declarative agents run on Copilot's orchestrator, they inherit Microsoft 365's compliance and responsible AI protections. Custom engine agents use their own orchestration, so the builder owns those controls. That adds governance work, the same tradeoff as any externally built agent, Genie-backed ones included.

questions.question: Which low-code tool does Microsoft position for building custom engine agents, as opposed to declarative agents?
choices: Copilot Studio
SharePoint agent creation
Agent Builder in Microsoft 365 Copilot
Work IQ Dev Tools
questions.explanation: Microsoft's tooling map: Agent Builder (low-code) and Work IQ Dev Tools (pro-code, declarative only) for declarative agents; Copilot Studio (low-code) or Visual Studio, VS Code and the Agents Toolkit (pro-code) for custom engine agents.

questions.question: Under the Copilot Studio billing rules, when are generative answers from an agent not charged even for a user without a Copilot license?
choices: When the agent uses a non-reasoning model such as GPT-5 chat instead of a reasoning model
When the agent is published only to Teams and SharePoint, regardless of how it was built
When the agent was created in Agent Builder in Microsoft 365 and the response doesn't use tenant graph grounding
Whenever the agent runs in Copilot Chat rather than Teams, because Copilot Chat generative answers are billed to the user's seat instead
questions.explanation: Footnote 2 of the billing rates: agents incur charges for generative answers unless the agent was created in Agent Builder in Microsoft 365 and the response doesn't use tenant graph grounding. As soon as the agent grounds on tenant data, the 10-credit tenant graph grounding meter applies for unlicensed users.

questions.question: In Microsoft Foundry Agent Service, what distinguishes a hosted agent from a prompt agent?
choices: A hosted agent has no Entra identity of its own, while a prompt agent always gets a dedicated identity
A hosted agent can only use OpenAI models, while a prompt agent can use any model in the Foundry catalog
A hosted agent runs your own code in a container and adds compute cost; Foundry runs a no-code prompt agent for you
A hosted agent is hosted by Microsoft in the customer's Microsoft 365 tenant, while a prompt agent runs in the customer's own Azure subscription
questions.explanation: Foundry Agent Service offers prompt agents (no code, Foundry runs them), voice prompt agents, and hosted agents (your container or package using frameworks such as Agent Framework, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK or Anthropic Agent SDK). Cost model: prompt agents bill per-call inference plus tool usage; hosted agents add container compute.

questions.question: Where can a Microsoft Foundry agent be published so that Microsoft 365 users can reach it?
choices: To Microsoft Copilot and Teams, and to the Entra Agent Registry
Only to Power Apps through a premium connector
Only to Copilot Studio, which must republish it as a declarative agent
Only to a custom web app; Foundry agents can't appear in Microsoft 365
questions.explanation: Foundry Agent Service supports sharing agents through Microsoft Copilot and Teams and the Entra Agent Registry. That gives pro-code teams a path into Microsoft 365 without Copilot Studio, but the Foundry inference and tool costs still apply alongside any Microsoft 365 licensing.

questions.question: Which interoperability protocol does Foundry Agent Service list as generally available at version 1.0 for agent-to-agent communication?
choices: Bot Framework Direct Line 3
A2A (Agent2Agent)
gRPC Agent Mesh
OpenAPI 4.0
questions.explanation: Foundry's overview states A2A v1.0 is generally available (v0.3 remains in preview), alongside MCP server tools. Open protocols like MCP and A2A are how non-Microsoft agents, Databricks Genie included, plug into Microsoft's estate without proprietary lock-in.

questions.question: Which Foundry agent type can't be published to Teams or Microsoft 365 Copilot as a text agent, according to the Foundry overview?
choices: Prompt agents that use MCP tools
Hosted agents built with LangGraph
Voice-based prompt agents (Voice Live)
Agents that use file search
questions.explanation: The Foundry overview notes that voice agents can't be published to Teams or Microsoft 365 Copilot as text agents. Check the channel story before a customer commits to a voice design.

questions.question: What does Microsoft's pricing page say about the cost of using Foundry itself?
choices: Foundry is included in every Microsoft 365 Copilot license, so agents carry no Azure cost
The platform is free to explore, and each feature (models, Agent Service, tools) is billed at its own rate
Foundry is billed as a flat monthly platform fee per project, which covers model tokens, Agent Service calls and every built-in tool
Foundry bills in Copilot Credits at the same rates as Copilot Studio's standard harness
questions.explanation: There is no single 'Foundry price'. The platform is free to explore, and each service has its own billing model: model inference by tokens, Agent Service by calls and tools, hosted agents by container compute. Don't quote one agent price for Foundry.

questions.question: How does Microsoft's Agent 365 documentation describe the product?
choices: As a model hosting service for running custom engine agents built with the Agents SDK
As a Microsoft 365 add-on that builds, hosts and runs agents for every department, replacing the need for Copilot Studio or Foundry
As the observability platform for AI: management, governance, security and business value for agents
As the consumer edition of Copilot for people signed in with personal Microsoft accounts
questions.explanation: Agent 365 is the control plane for agents: an agent registry in the Microsoft 365 admin center, Agent Map, connected platforms for third-party agents, approval workflows, finding ownerless agents, risk signals from Defender, Entra and Purview, and Copilot Credits cost management. It doesn't build agents.

questions.question: Which agents can Agent 365 bring into its registry and governance, per Microsoft's GA announcement?
choices: Only agents built in Copilot Studio or Foundry inside the same Microsoft 365 tenant
Microsoft, partner and third-party agents across SaaS, cloud and local environments
Only declarative agents that an admin has approved and published to the Agent Store
Only agents running on Windows 365 Cloud PCs that are joined to Microsoft Entra ID
questions.explanation: Agent 365 is meant to cover agents wherever they're built, including SaaS, cloud and local agents, using either their own access or delegated access. Connected platforms bring in agents from other vendors. That framing lets a customer govern a Genie-backed agent alongside Copilot agents instead of treating 'Microsoft-native' as a governance requirement.

questions.question: What did Microsoft announce at Ignite 2026 about Entra Agent ID and local agents?
choices: Entra Agent ID will stop supporting local agents, so tools like GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code must authenticate as the signed-in user
Entra Agent ID was retired in favor of plain service principals for all non-Microsoft agents
Local agents are now blocked by default on every Intune-managed Windows and macOS device
Entra will assign agent identities to discovered local agents such as GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code (preview)
questions.explanation: At Ignite 2026 Microsoft extended Entra Agent ID to discovered local agents, naming GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code, in preview. Defender added runtime protection for local agents and Intune previewed local AI agent governance. Microsoft is positioning its identity and security stack to govern non-Microsoft agents, which helps a multi-vendor agent strategy.

questions.question: How does Windows 365 for Agents relate to Copilot Studio after Ignite 2026?
choices: It's a separate Windows 365 SKU priced per Cloud PC, and Copilot Studio agents can use it only if every user has a Windows 365 license
It's available as a computer-use tool in the standard harness and is eligible for Copilot Credits
It replaces Copilot Studio as the only supported runtime for all autonomous agents
It's included free with every Microsoft 365 Copilot license, with no credit consumption
questions.explanation: Per the Book of News, Windows 365 for Agents is available as a computer-use tool in Copilot Studio's standard harness (preview in the Copilot harness from December) and is eligible for Copilot Credits. Computer use is billed: computer-using agents bill at the agent action rate and aren't covered by the Microsoft 365 Copilot inclusion.

questions.question: Microsoft's September 2026 Copilot Credits guidance splits Copilot into two consumption tracks. What are they?
choices: 'Everyday AI' included in the seat (within limits) and 'advanced AI' billed in Copilot Credits
'Seat AI' covering everything in the Microsoft 365 apps and 'Azure AI' for anything built in Foundry, with no Copilot Credits involved at all
'Chat AI' billed per message and 'Agent AI' billed at a flat fee per agent per month
'Basic AI' for E3 customers and 'Premium AI' for E5 and E7 customers, both priced per user
questions.explanation: Everyday AI (Copilot Chat, Copilot in the Office apps, Auto model selection and similar) is included with the user subscription license, subject to applicable limits. Advanced AI, meaning long-running agentic work such as Cowork, Code, Autopilot, advanced SharePoint and OneDrive work, and some frontier models, requires usage-based billing in Copilot Credits. The $30 seat no longer covers everything.

questions.question: Which of these is listed by Microsoft as a usage-based (Copilot Credits) service, not covered by the Copilot seat alone?
choices: Copilot in Word summarizing an open document
Copilot in Outlook drafting an email reply
Teams Phone Agent and intelligent call delegation
Copilot Chat answering a web-grounded question
questions.explanation: Microsoft's usage-based billing overview lists services managed by Copilot Credits, including Cowork, advanced work in SharePoint and OneDrive, Work IQ API, Copilot Managed Runtime, Teams Phone Agent, Code, Autopilot, intelligent call delegation, consecutive interpretation, video creation and Copilot Studio. Everyday drafting and summarizing in the Office apps stays in the license.

questions.question: What is the default state of pay-as-you-go agents for Copilot Chat (Basic) and Microsoft 365 Copilot (Basic) users?
choices: Turned off by default until an admin sets up billing and turns them on
On by default, free for the first 1,000 Copilot Credits each month
On by default for every Basic user, billed to the tenant's first Azure subscription until an admin opts out
Permanently unavailable; Basic users can never use metered agents
questions.explanation: Microsoft's agent management page says pay-as-you-go agents are turned off by default for Basic users, and the pay-as-you-go overview says PAYG billing is disabled by default. Nothing is metered until an admin links a billing policy to an Azure subscription and connects it to the service.

questions.question: What can a user do with a Copilot Studio trial license?
choices: Publish up to three agents to Teams, free for the first 90 days
Build and test agents in the test chat panel, but not publish them
Use premium connectors in production with a 25,000-credit allowance
Publish to any channel, but only for 30 days before agents expire
questions.explanation: The trial is for individuals to build and test in the test panel. Microsoft is explicit that you can't publish the agent. A successful pilot still needs a funded billing setup before anyone else can use what was built.

questions.question: The Copilot Studio user license for makers is free. What tenant-level prerequisite does Microsoft attach to getting it?
choices: Every maker must also hold a Power Apps Premium per-user license
The tenant needs at least one Microsoft 365 Copilot license assigned to each maker
The tenant must first join the Frontier early-access program
The tenant needs a prepaid Copilot Credit pack subscription first
questions.explanation: Microsoft's licensing page lists the Copilot Studio user license as free, assigned by an admin, but requiring a tenant prepaid Copilot Credit pack subscription. Separately, a Microsoft 365 Copilot license lets users build agents for the Microsoft Copilot harness, and admins can grant pay-as-you-go authoring access through the Copilot Studio authors security group.

questions.question: How is Microsoft 365 Copilot (the enterprise Premium experience) sold to a commercial customer that already has Microsoft 365 E5?
choices: As a consumption-only service billed per prompt in credits
It's already included in E5, so no extra license is needed
As an add-on license on top of an eligible base plan
Only as part of an upgrade to the Microsoft 365 E7 suite
questions.explanation: Microsoft's license comparison shows Copilot as 'available as an add-on' for E3 and E5, and included in E7. Eligible base plans include Microsoft 365 E3, E5, E7, F1, F3, Business Basic, Standard and Premium, Apps for enterprise and business, and Office 365 E1, E3 and E5, among others.

questions.question: What is the widely cited US list price of the enterprise Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on?
choices: $21 per user per month
$15 per user per month
$99 per user per month
$30 per user per month
questions.explanation: Microsoft 365 Copilot is $30 per user per month. $21 is Copilot Business (SMB), $15 is Agent 365 standalone, and $99 is the Microsoft 365 E7 bundle. Remember that the seat price covers 'everyday AI' only. Advanced, agentic experiences are metered in Copilot Credits on top.

questions.question: Which organizations is Microsoft 365 Copilot Business designed for?
choices: Any organization of any size that prefers to pay monthly instead of annually
Enterprises with more than 300 Microsoft 365 E3 or E5 seats in the tenant
Organizations with up to 300 users on eligible Microsoft 365 Business plans
Education and nonprofit tenants only, at a discounted academic rate
questions.explanation: Copilot Business is an add-on for organizations with up to 300 users on eligible Microsoft 365 Business plans (Business Basic, Standard, Premium, Apps for Business, Teams Essentials). Microsoft says it provides the same Copilot capabilities, with licensing and purchasing options designed for SMBs, and an annual commitment. Above 300 users, Microsoft points customers to the enterprise options.

questions.question: What did Microsoft list as the price of Copilot Business when it became generally available in December 2025?
choices: $21 per user per month
$30 per user per month
$18 per user per month
$25 per user per month
questions.explanation: Microsoft announced Copilot Business at $21 per user per month. A limited-time promotion through June 30, 2026 took the add-on to $18 (about 15% off). Microsoft's March 2026 post confirmed Copilot Business 'remains $21' after the July 1, 2026 changes.

questions.question: What happened to Microsoft 365 Business + Copilot Business bundle prices on July 1, 2026?
choices: All three bundles fell by 15%, because the launch promotion was made permanent
Basic + Copilot rose $27→$28, Standard + Copilot $33.50→$35, Premium + Copilot stayed $43
All three bundles rose by exactly $3 per user per month, matching the E3 and E5 increases
The bundles were discontinued, so Copilot Business must now be bought separately
questions.explanation: Microsoft's 'lock in current pricing' post listed the July 1, 2026 bundle changes: Basic + Copilot Business $27 to $28, Standard + Copilot Business $33.50 to $35, Premium + Copilot Business unchanged at $43. Copilot Business alone stayed at $21. Customers buying before July 1 could lock in the earlier prices and promos.

questions.question: What does Microsoft 365 E7, the 'Frontier Suite', bundle?
choices: Microsoft 365 E5, Copilot Studio capacity packs, Fabric F64 capacity and Security Copilot
Microsoft 365 E3, Copilot Business, Defender Suite and unlimited Copilot Credits
Microsoft 365 E5, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Microsoft Entra Suite and Microsoft Agent 365
Microsoft 365 E5, GitHub Copilot Enterprise, Foundry credits and Power Apps Premium
questions.explanation: E7 went GA on May 1, 2026 at $99 per user per month and bundles M365 E5, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Entra Suite and Agent 365. It is available with and without Teams. It doesn't include agent consumption: Copilot Studio, Cowork and Foundry usage are still metered.

questions.question: A customer assumes E7 at $99 covers the cost of running their agents. What's the gotcha?
choices: E7 includes agent consumption but leaves out the Microsoft 365 Copilot license itself
E7 covers user licenses and governance; agent consumption is still billed separately
E7 includes 25,000 Copilot Credits per user per month, so heavy users rarely pay extra
E7 covers agent costs only when every single user in the tenant is licensed for E7
questions.explanation: Microsoft's E7 materials describe the bundle components, and nothing in them covers Copilot Credits or Foundry consumption. Independent analysts stress the same point: building and running agents still needs consumption spend through Copilot Studio, usage-based billing or Foundry. Model the per-user license and the usage meter separately.

questions.question: Using list prices after July 1, 2026, how much does E7 ($99) cost compared with buying E5 plus the Copilot add-on separately?
choices: About $9 more per user per month, since E5 ($60) plus Copilot ($30) is $90
About $39 more, because E5 and Copilot together list at $60 per user per month
About $18 less, because E5 ($87 after July 2026) plus Copilot ($30) is $117
The same, because E7 is simply Microsoft's new name for E5 plus the Copilot add-on
questions.explanation: E5 moved to $60 on July 1, 2026, and Copilot is $30, so $90 for the pair. E7 at $99 adds Agent 365 ($15 standalone) and Entra Suite for about $9 more. The bundle saves money only if the customer actually wants Agent 365 and Entra Suite for those users. Microsoft says E7 can be mixed with other licenses, so not every user needs it.

questions.question: Can a customer license only some users with Microsoft 365 E7 and keep others on E3 or E5?
choices: Only if at least 300 users in the tenant are moved onto E7 together
Only in tenants that buy the 'without Teams' edition of the E7 suite
No. Once purchased, E7 must cover every licensed user in the tenant
Yes. Licenses can be mixed, so E7 can go only to the users who need it
questions.explanation: Microsoft confirmed that organizations can mix licenses and not every user needs E7. A common pattern: E7 for heavy Copilot users and agent owners, E3 or E5 plus Copilot Chat (Basic) for everyone else, with Genie available to all through the Teams app.

questions.question: How is Agent 365 licensed as a standalone product?
choices: $15 per user per month
$0.01 per agent action
$15 per agent per month
Free with any Copilot Studio capacity pack
questions.explanation: Agent 365 became GA on May 1, 2026 and is licensed per user ($15 per user per month standalone) or through E7. Even though it governs agents, the license unit is the human user, which matters when a customer has few users and many agents, or the reverse.

questions.question: According to the Entra Agent ID documentation, what licensing is needed to extend Microsoft Entra security features (such as Conditional Access) to agents?
choices: Entra ID P1 alone
Defender for Cloud Apps
A Copilot Studio capacity pack
Microsoft Agent 365
questions.explanation: Entra Agent ID gives agents identities, but Microsoft states that extending Entra security features to agents requires Microsoft Agent 365. Agent 365 is included in E7 and sold as an add-on to E5, A5 or Business Premium (or with Defender Suite plus Purview Suite). Budget for it when 'govern our agents' shows up in requirements.

questions.question: Which industry analyst firm called Agent 365 'a work in progress with limited net new functionality' for its price at launch?
choices: Everest Group
Gartner
IDC
Forrester
questions.explanation: Gartner, quoted by The Register in March 2026, called Agent 365 a work in progress and advised that upgrading to E7 just for Agent 365 wasn't recommended until Microsoft adds value. Use this carefully with customers: it's a reason to make Microsoft prove the value per user, not a reason to dismiss governance.

questions.question: How much Security Copilot capacity does Microsoft include for eligible Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 customers?
choices: 400 Security Compute Units per month for every 1,000 paid user licenses, up to 10,000 SCUs per month
Unlimited SCUs, as long as the tenant's usage stays within Microsoft's fair-use policy
A flat 100 SCUs per tenant per month, regardless of how many E5 licenses it has
One Security Compute Unit per paid E5 user each month, pooled across the tenant, with no upper cap for very large organizations
questions.explanation: Microsoft includes 400 SCUs each month per 1,000 paid E5 or E7 licenses, up to 10,000 SCUs a month, at no extra cost. For example, 4,000 licenses gives 1,600 SCUs. SCUs reset monthly and don't roll over. Microsoft says usage beyond the allocation may be charged in future at $6 per SCU pay-as-you-go, with 30 days' notice.

questions.question: A customer with 400 E5 licenses asks how much included Security Copilot capacity they get. What's the answer?
choices: None, because there's a 1,000-license minimum
40 SCUs per month
160 SCUs per month
400 SCUs per month
questions.explanation: The allocation is pro-rated: 400 SCUs per 1,000 licenses means 400 licenses gives 160 SCUs a month, which is Microsoft's own example. There's no minimum license count, but Sentinel customers without E5 or E7 aren't eligible.

questions.question: How does a tenant become entitled to SharePoint Advanced Management (SAM) for Copilot deployments?
choices: It requires a Copilot Studio capacity pack to be active somewhere in the tenant
Every user must hold a separate SAM add-on license costing $3 per user per month
It's included only in Microsoft 365 E5 Compliance and the Purview Suite add-on
Once at least one user has a Microsoft 365 Copilot license (or via SAM Plan 1 or E7)
questions.explanation: SAM's prerequisites say it's available when at least one user is assigned a Microsoft 365 Copilot license, or with the SAM Plan 1 add-on, or with E7. Some features, such as restricted site creation, still need the Plan 1 add-on. SAM's oversharing tools (data access governance reports, site access reviews, Restricted Access Control, Restricted Content Discovery) should be part of every Copilot readiness plan.

questions.question: Which experiences does Microsoft's usage-based billing overview mark as 'Copilot license required' even though they're also metered in Copilot Credits?
choices: Security Copilot promptbooks run by SOC analysts in Defender
Copilot Chat web-grounded prompts and Edge sidebar chat
Copilot Studio agents published to a public website
Cowork, advanced work in SharePoint and OneDrive, and Code
questions.explanation: Some advanced experiences need both a Copilot seat and credits. Microsoft's usage-based billing overview lists Cowork, advanced SharePoint and OneDrive work, and Code as 'Copilot license required'. So a Cowork user costs a $30 seat plus metered usage, which upends a seat-only business case.

questions.question: What is the list price of a Copilot Studio Copilot Credit capacity pack in the US?
choices: $200 per pack per month for 25,000 Copilot Credits, billed annually
$30 per pack per month for 25,000 credits, billed monthly
$200 per maker per month, with unlimited credits for their agents
$2,000 per tenant per year for 1,000,000 credits, billed upfront
questions.explanation: Microsoft's Copilot Studio pricing page lists capacity packs of 25,000 Copilot Credits at $200 per pack per month (billed annually). That works out to $0.008 per credit, versus $0.01 pay-as-you-go. Unused pack credits don't roll over to the next month.

questions.question: What does Microsoft include with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license for Copilot Studio agents?
choices: A free Copilot Studio capacity pack of 25,000 credits per month for every 10 Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses the tenant has purchased
Nothing; all Copilot Studio usage requires separately purchased Copilot Credits
Agent capabilities in Copilot Studio when used in Microsoft Copilot, Teams or SharePoint, under the user's identity
Unlimited Copilot Studio agents on any channel, including public websites and WhatsApp
questions.explanation: The Copilot Studio licensing page lists 'agent capabilities in Copilot Studio when used in Microsoft Copilot, Teams, or SharePoint' as included with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license. Classic answers, generative answers and tenant Graph grounding aren't charged when the agent runs with the licensed user's identity, subject to fair use. Public-website or autonomous scenarios fall outside that.

questions.question: What was the reported change to Microsoft 365 E5 list pricing on July 1, 2026?
choices: E5 fell to $54 to make room for E7
E5 rose to $69 and now includes Copilot
E5 rose from $57 to $60 per user per month
E5 stayed at $57 and E3 rose to $39
questions.explanation: E5 went from $57 to $60 per user per month on July 1, 2026, and E3 from $36 to $39, as part of Microsoft's broader commercial price update. That moves the E5 + Copilot list total to $90, which is the comparison point for the $99 E7 bundle.

questions.question: Per Agent 365's overview, what licensing is needed for a tenant to start using Agent 365?
choices: Any Copilot Studio capacity pack unlocks Agent 365 for the tenant
At least one user needs a qualifying Agent 365 license; it's sold per user
None. It's free for every Microsoft 365 tenant with Entra ID P1
Every agent listed in the registry needs its own Agent 365 license, billed per agent per month
questions.explanation: Agent 365 is generally available for the commercial segment on a per-user basis. Microsoft notes it works best with E5 and that at least one user needs a qualifying license. In planning, separate who needs the governance controls (admins, agent owners) from who uses agents.

questions.question: What limited-time promotion did Microsoft run on the standalone Copilot Business add-on through June 30, 2026?
choices: $10 instead of $21 per user per month
Free with any purchase of Business Premium
Free for the first 12 months for up to 300 users
$18 instead of $21 per user per month (about 15% off)
questions.explanation: Microsoft's March 2026 post listed the Copilot Business add-on at $18 instead of $21 (about 15% off) until June 30, 2026, with larger discounts on some Business plan bundles (up to 35%). Microsoft promotions are frequent; ask what discount and price-protection terms the customer's account team is offering.

questions.question: What did Microsoft say about how E7's price compares with buying its components individually?
choices: That it's priced the same as à la carte but adds unlimited Copilot Credits
That it includes a guaranteed 40% discount for every customer
That it's priced below purchasing those capabilities à la carte
That it's priced above à la carte because of included consulting
questions.explanation: Microsoft's GA post says E7 is priced below buying the capabilities à la carte, without giving a percentage. Gartner put the discount at roughly 13% and argued bigger bundles should get bigger discounts. The real question is whether each E7 user needs all four components.

questions.question: Which channel does Microsoft's Copilot Studio licensing page say a Microsoft 365 Copilot license lets users build agents for?
choices: Dynamics 365 Contact Center
The customer conversation harness for external websites
Azure Bot Service Direct Line only
The Microsoft Copilot harness
questions.explanation: Copilot Studio's licensing page lists the Microsoft 365 Copilot license as letting users build agents for the Microsoft Copilot harness. Building is one thing. Running those agents for unlicensed users, autonomously, or on external channels still consumes credits.

questions.question: In the Copilot Studio standard-harness billing table, how many Copilot Credits does a generative answer cost?
choices: 2 Copilot Credits
10 Copilot Credits
5 Copilot Credits
1 Copilot Credit
questions.explanation: Core rates: classic answer 1, generative answer 2, agent action 5, tenant graph grounding 10. A single interaction can hit several meters, for example a grounded generative answer is 2 + 10 = 12 credits.

questions.question: What does one 'agent action' cost in Copilot Studio?
choices: 13 Copilot Credits
5 Copilot Credits
2 Copilot Credits
1 Copilot Credit per 100 actions
questions.explanation: An agent action is 5 credits. Microsoft counts triggers, deep reasoning steps, topic transitions and tool or connector calls shown on the activity map as agent actions. Each Genie tool call from a Copilot Studio agent counts here, on top of any generative answer.

questions.question: What does tenant graph grounding add to a Copilot Studio response for an unlicensed user?
choices: Nothing; grounding is always free
10 Copilot Credits
30 Copilot Credits
2 Copilot Credits
questions.explanation: Tenant graph grounding is 10 credits per use. Microsoft's example: an agent grounded on the tenant graph uses 12 credits for one complex prompt (10 for grounding + 2 for the generative answer). Older documents listed this at 30 'messages', before the September 2025 rename to Copilot Credits.

questions.question: How are Copilot Studio agent flow actions billed?
choices: Under Power Automate per-user licensing, not credits
1 Copilot Credit per flow run regardless of length
13 Copilot Credits per 100 agent flow actions
5 Copilot Credits per action, like an agent action
questions.explanation: Agent flows bill 13 credits per 100 actions. Each trigger execution counts as one agent flow action, including failed polling-trigger evaluations that don't start a run, so a polling trigger can cost money while doing nothing. Classic Power Automate cloud flows still use Power Automate licensing, not credits.

questions.question: A Copilot Studio agent uses a document-extraction ('content processing') tool on a 40-page PDF. What does the billing table charge for that processing?
choices: 320 Copilot Credits, at 8 credits per page
Nothing, because content processing is included
5 Copilot Credits, as one agent action
40 Copilot Credits, at 1 credit per page
questions.explanation: Content processing tools bill 8 credits per page: 40 × 8 = 320 credits, about $3.20 at PAYG list. Document-heavy agents (invoices, contracts) are easy to under-budget because the per-page meter dwarfs the conversation meters.

questions.question: How is voice billed for Copilot Studio agents using generative AI voice (not premium)?
choices: Voice itself isn't billed; only the transcript's generative answers are
35 Copilot Credits per minute, with the core answer or action activity included
2 Copilot Credits per spoken response, the same as a text generative answer, regardless of how long the call lasts
10 Copilot Credits per minute, the same rate for every type of voice
questions.explanation: Voice is per minute: classic voice 10, GenAI voice 35, premium GenAI voice 75 credits per minute, with the underlying classic or generative answer or agent action 'included'. A 6-minute GenAI voice call is about 210 credits ($2.10 PAYG) before any premium model tokens.

questions.question: When a Copilot Studio agent uses a reasoning-capable model, how is it billed?
choices: Only per token at the premium rate, with the normal feature rates waived entirely
At a flat 100 credits per conversation, regardless of how many tokens or turns are used
Two meters: the feature rate plus premium AI tools at 10 credits per 1,000 billed tokens
At the standard feature rate only, because reasoning and thinking tokens are never billed
questions.explanation: Reasoning models add a premium token meter on top of the normal feature rates: 10 credits per 1,000 billed tokens. Output and reasoning tokens are billed, cache writes are billed as input, and cache reads are not. GPT-5 chat isn't classed as a reasoning model, so it incurs only the feature rate.

questions.question: In Microsoft's reasoning-model example, which tokens are not billed?
choices: Input tokens read from the prompt cache
Output tokens
Reasoning (thinking) tokens
Input tokens written to the cache
questions.explanation: Microsoft's worked example: cache reads aren't billed, but cache writes are billed as input, and output and reasoning tokens are billed. A new conversation that must write a large context to cache can cost several times more than a follow-up turn. The example went from 141 to 461 premium credits for a fresh conversation.

questions.question: How are computer-using agents (CUA) in Copilot Studio billed for a Microsoft 365 Copilot licensed user?
choices: At the agent action rate. CUA isn't covered by the Microsoft 365 Copilot inclusion
At the classic answer rate of 1 credit per step, since no LLM is involved
Nothing, because computer use runs on a Windows 365 Cloud PC whose license already covers the agent's automation steps
Per hour of Windows 365 Cloud PC time only, with no credit charge at all
questions.explanation: Footnote 4: computer-using agents bill at the agent action rate and aren't covered by the Microsoft 365 Copilot license inclusion. UI automation steps add up quickly, and licensed users don't make them free.

questions.question: A team wants to use a bring-your-own model (for example a Foundry model) in Copilot Studio. How is that model's usage billed?
choices: Separately, outside the Copilot Credit rate table
Free, because the customer already pays Azure
At the same rate as GPT-5 chat
At the premium AI tools rate of 10 credits per 1,000 tokens
questions.explanation: Microsoft excludes bring-your-own-model configurations, including Foundry models, from these rates. They're billed separately on the Azure side, while the Copilot Studio feature meters (answers, actions) still apply. That's two bills for one agent, so FinOps needs both.

questions.question: Under what condition is a Copilot Studio agent's usage not charged for a user who holds a Microsoft 365 Copilot license?
choices: Only when the agent uses classic topics and never calls generative AI features
Whenever any licensed user created the agent, no matter who ends up using it
Whenever the agent was built by someone with a Copilot license, regardless of who uses it or which channel it's published to
When the agent runs under that licensed user's own authenticated identity (within fair use)
questions.explanation: Footnote 1: usage is included when the agent user is licensed and the agent operates using the authenticated Microsoft Copilot user's identity, which Microsoft frames as business-to-employee scenarios, subject to fair usage limits. Autonomous runs, external customers, and some features (CUA, non-agent-triggered flows) don't qualify.

questions.question: An autonomous Copilot Studio agent fires on a new email and calls an agent flow. Every user in the tenant has Microsoft 365 Copilot. Is the flow billed?
choices: No, as long as the agent itself is published to Teams or Copilot Chat
No. Once every user holds a Microsoft 365 Copilot license, the tenant is exempt from all Copilot Studio agent and flow billing
Only if the flow runs for longer than five minutes before it completes
Yes. Autonomously triggered runs consume Copilot Credits even if all users are licensed
questions.explanation: Microsoft is explicit: agent flow runs called by an autonomous agent consume credits even if the users have Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses. The exemption is tied to a licensed user interacting under their identity. Event triggers have no user, so there's no exemption. Microsoft's order-processing example bills 20 credits a day for a simple autonomous agent.

questions.question: For agent flows, which trigger keeps a licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot user's flow runs at no charge?
choices: 'When an agent calls the flow', with the user authenticated and licensed
'When a new email arrives', as long as the mailbox belongs to a licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot user
A scheduled recurrence trigger owned by the licensed user
'When an item is created' in a SharePoint list the user owns
questions.explanation: Only flows triggered by 'When an agent calls the flow', in a conversation with a licensed and authenticated user, are no charge. Other triggers, including calls to agents from inside a flow, consume credits at the standard rate. Check trigger types when estimating agent flow costs.

questions.question: Microsoft's 'sales performance agent' example has 50 licensed and 100 unlicensed users, each asking 4 tenant-grounded questions in Copilot Chat. Which users drive the bill?
choices: Neither group, because agents in Copilot Chat are always free of charge
Only the 50 licensed users, because unlicensed users can't use agents
All 150 users: [(4×2)+(4×10)] × 150 = 7,200 credits in total
Only the 100 unlicensed users: [(4×2)+(4×10)] × 100 = 4,800 credits
questions.explanation: Licensed users interacting under their own identity aren't charged, so only the 100 unlicensed users count: 4 generative answers at 2 credits plus 4 tenant graph groundings at 10 credits, which is 48 credits per user, or 4,800 total. Grounding is 5× the answer cost, so grounding drives this bill.

questions.question: If a tenant runs out of prepaid Copilot Studio capacity, what does Microsoft say may happen to users with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license?
choices: They might not be blocked, since their in-scope usage isn't drawing on capacity
They're switched to pay-as-you-go automatically at double the normal rate
They're blocked first, so remaining capacity is saved for unlicensed users
Their Copilot licenses are suspended until the capacity has been restored
questions.explanation: When enforcement kicks in, agents are blocked for capacity-consuming usage, but Microsoft notes licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot users 'might not be blocked'. A capacity incident can therefore look partial: some people are blocked, others aren't.

questions.question: At what point does Copilot Studio technically enforce prepaid capacity and start blocking agents?
choices: At 100% of prepaid capacity, with no grace period
When tenant usage reaches 125% of prepaid capacity
Never. Overage is only ever billed, never blocked
At 150% of prepaid capacity, after a 30-day notice
questions.explanation: Enforcement triggers at 125% of prepaid capacity. Agents in affected environments are blocked, including conversations in progress, with a message like 'This agent is currently unavailable. It has reached its usage limit.' Admins get email and a Power Platform admin center notice. Fixes: reallocate, buy more, or add pay-as-you-go.

questions.question: A tenant pool is at 125% and enforcement has started. Environment A has its own 10,000-credit allocation with credits left. What happens to agents in Environment A?
choices: They keep running while Environment A still has allocation left
They automatically draw from other environments' allocations
They're blocked with everything else in the tenant
They run at reduced speed until month end
questions.explanation: Microsoft's allocation example: environments without allocation draw from the tenant pool and are enforced with it, but an environment with its own allocation isn't enforced while that allocation lasts. Allocating capacity to business-critical environments is a way to protect them from noisy neighbors.

questions.question: How does adding pay-as-you-go change what happens when prepaid Copilot Studio credits run out?
choices: PAYG replaces the prepaid pack entirely, and the unused pack balance is refunded
PAYG keeps agents running but bills all overage at double the normal per-credit rate
Nothing changes: agents are still blocked at 125% of prepaid capacity, and PAYG only covers usage from the following month onward
Agents aren't blocked; uncovered usage is billed to the PAYG plan (unless an admin limit is set to stop)
questions.explanation: With overage billed to PAYG, running out of prepaid credits doesn't block agents: the excess goes to the Azure-billed plan. Agents an admin turned off, or that hit a monthly limit set to stop, are still blocked. PAYG keeps agents up but makes spend open-ended unless you set limits.

questions.question: What happens to unused Copilot Studio prepaid credits at the end of a month?
choices: They're refunded at month end as Azure account credit
They roll over and stay usable for up to 12 months
They expire; capacity is enforced monthly with no carry-over
They're moved automatically into the tenant's P3 pool
questions.explanation: Microsoft: 'Copilot Studio enforces purchased capacity monthly, and unused Copilot Credits don't carry over to the next month.' Buying packs for peak months wastes money in quiet months. PAYG or a P3 annual pool can fit spiky usage better.

questions.question: When agent-flow enforcement is triggered for lack of credits, what happens to the parent agent?
choices: Only new flow runs are blocked; the agent keeps answering interactions that don't need the flow
The agent falls back to classic topic answers only until the credits renew
The entire agent is unpublished, including in-progress conversations, and stays offline until an admin republishes it manually
In-flight and new flow runs are queued and replayed automatically next month
questions.explanation: Agent flow enforcement blocks new flow runs only. The parent agent keeps answering non-flow interactions, and the block resets monthly when prepaid credits renew. Users get partial functionality, and the cause can be hard to spot.

questions.question: An admin sets a monthly credit limit on a Copilot Studio agent in the admin center. Does that limit stop the agent flows the agent calls?
choices: No. Monthly agent limits don't stop the agent flows it calls
Yes. All downstream flows stop when the agent hits its limit
Only flows in the same solution are stopped
Only if the flows use premium connectors
questions.explanation: Microsoft calls this out: monthly limits set on an agent in the admin center don't stop the agent flows it calls. Flows need their own controls.

questions.question: What is the pay-as-you-go list price of one Copilot Credit?
questions.explanation: PAYG is $0.01 per Copilot Credit, billed in arrears monthly through an Azure subscription. Capacity packs work out to $0.008 per credit ($200 / 25,000), and P3 tiers discount 5% to 20% off PAYG.

questions.question: How is Copilot Studio pay-as-you-go billing set up?
choices: By adding a corporate credit card to each agent's billing settings in Copilot Studio, which charges per conversation at month end
Through a billing policy in the Power Platform admin center that links environments to an Azure subscription
Automatically, for every tenant that already has an active Azure subscription
Through Microsoft 365 Copilot seat assignment in the Microsoft 365 admin center
questions.explanation: Copilot Studio PAYG uses a Power Platform billing policy tied to an Azure subscription. Linking an environment turns on the Azure meters, and unlinking stops billing. Usage over the included amounts in linked environments flows to that subscription.

questions.question: Do Copilot Credits bought pay-as-you-go or through P3 count toward a customer's Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment (MACC)?
choices: Only PAYG counts; P3 is excluded
No. Copilot Credits are Microsoft 365 spend and never count toward MACC
Yes. Microsoft's guidance says both PAYG and P3 decrement MACC
Only P3 counts; PAYG is excluded
questions.explanation: Microsoft's Copilot Credits guidance states both pay-as-you-go and the P3 pre-purchase plan decrement the MACC. Customers with Azure commitments can fund agent consumption from them. The same applies to Databricks on Azure, which is also MACC-eligible, so it's worth surfacing when comparing Genie and Copilot TCO.

questions.question: For Copilot Chat (Basic) users, which agents are included at no charge?
choices: Agents grounded on Graph connectors, as long as the user has E5
Any agent built in Agent Builder, including SharePoint-grounded ones
Any agent that IT has approved and published to the Agent Store
Declarative agents grounded only in instructions and public websites
questions.explanation: Declarative agents grounded in instructions and public websites are included with Copilot Chat (Basic). Agents that access shared tenant data, such as SharePoint or Copilot connector content, are billed by metered consumption. Grounding an agent on the intranet turns a free agent into a metered one for every unlicensed user.

questions.question: Where is the billing policy for Copilot Chat pay-as-you-go agents created?
choices: In Copilot Studio, under each agent's Settings > Billing page
In the Microsoft 365 admin center, linked to an Azure subscription in the same tenant
In the Azure portal under Reservations, where it's purchased as a one-year commitment and linked to Copilot Chat users
In the Microsoft Purview portal, under Data Security Posture Management
questions.explanation: Admins (Billing, AI or Global Administrator) create a billing policy in the Microsoft 365 admin center, choose users or groups, optionally set a budget, and connect it under Copilot > Billing & usage > Pay-as-you-go services. You need an Azure subscription and resource group in the same tenant. A tenant can have up to 50 billing policies.

questions.question: An admin sets a $5,000 budget on a Copilot Chat pay-as-you-go billing policy. What happens when usage passes $5,000?
choices: Usage is throttled to classic answers only until the next billing month
Usage continues. Microsoft says the system doesn't enforce that budget; it only notifies
The overage is waived and absorbed by Microsoft as a goodwill credit
All metered agents stop immediately for every user covered by the billing policy until the next billing month begins
questions.explanation: Microsoft's PAYG setup page says the system doesn't enforce the budget, and usage continues after it's passed. To cap spend you need a different control, such as a spending policy with a limited monthly budget in Copilot Cost Management, or narrower user scoping.

questions.question: After an admin disconnects a Copilot Chat pay-as-you-go billing policy, how long can users keep using metered agents?
choices: Up to about two hours
Until the end of the billing month
Until they sign out and back in
It stops instantly with no lag
questions.explanation: Microsoft notes it can take up to two hours for users to lose access after a policy is disconnected. Metered usage in that window still bills, so plan cutovers accordingly.

questions.question: A tenant connects a billing policy covering a specific user group, but an 'all users' policy is already connected. What does Microsoft tell admins to do?
choices: Nothing. Microsoft automatically applies the more specific user-group policy and ignores the all-users policy for those users
Disconnect the existing 'all users' policy before connecting the user-specific one
Delete the Azure subscription that's linked to the all-users policy
Open a support ticket so Microsoft can merge the two policies
questions.explanation: Connecting a policy gives access to all users it covers. Microsoft says to disconnect any existing 'all users' policy before connecting a user-specific one. Otherwise everyone still has access, which defeats a scoped pilot.

questions.question: Roughly how many credits does Microsoft say a test prompt to a built-in agent like 'Writing Coach' consumes when validating PAYG setup?
choices: About 100 credits
Nothing. Test prompts are free
About 12 credits
About 1 credit
questions.explanation: Microsoft's setup page says a test prompt to Learning Coach, Writing Coach or Career Coach consumes about 12 credits, which matches a grounded generative answer (2 + 10). Small per prompt, but multiply by users × prompts × working days.

questions.question: In Microsoft 365 Copilot Cost Management, what happens when users reach a policy's 'Limited monthly budget'?
choices: Nothing happens; the limited monthly budget only sends an alert email
They're automatically moved to the next spending policy in priority order
They lose access to covered agents and services until credits reset on the 1st
They can keep working, but are switched to a lower-cost model for the month
questions.explanation: The policy-level limited monthly budget is a hard cap: users lose access for the rest of the month until credits reset. Users at a per-user limit can request more credits. They don't fall through to other policies, because each user is assigned to exactly one policy.

questions.question: A user is covered by two spending policies with different limits. How does Copilot Cost Management decide which applies?
choices: The user is blocked from all metered services until an admin resolves the overlap
Both policies apply, and their limits are added together into one larger budget
The policy with the lowest limit always wins, as the safer of the two choices
They're assigned one policy (highest per-user limit wins); limits aren't combined
questions.explanation: Overlapping policies don't stack. Microsoft assigns the user to a single policy by highest per-user limit, then largest policy limit, then most recently created. Design policies as non-overlapping tiers to avoid surprises.

questions.question: Why can a user sometimes start new Cowork tasks after their spending limit has already been reached?
choices: Users with E5 licenses bypass spending limits for the first 24 hours
Limits are only checked once a week, when the usage report runs
Credit consumption and limit enforcement are evaluated asynchronously
Spending limits apply only to Copilot Studio agents, not to Cowork
questions.explanation: Microsoft states consumption and enforcement are evaluated asynchronously, so tasks can start after a limit is reached, before enforcement takes effect. Treat limits as near-real-time guardrails, not exact ceilings, and leave headroom.

questions.question: What is the default for the 'Auto-apply new services' setting on spending policies, and why does it matter?
choices: On, but only for services that Microsoft classifies as 'everyday AI'
On by default, so new usage-based services Microsoft releases join existing policies automatically
Off by default, so new metered services stay blocked for everyone until an admin adds them to a spending policy one at a time
There's no such setting; every new service must be approved one by one
questions.explanation: Auto-apply new services is on by default. When Microsoft ships a new metered service, users in existing policies can start consuming it. Customers who want deliberate rollout should turn it off and add services manually.

questions.question: A customer configures a Microsoft 365 resource-based spending policy for a Copilot Studio environment that already has Power Platform billing policies. What happens?
choices: The Microsoft 365 policy takes precedence; Power Platform allocations stop applying there
The Power Platform billing policy always wins for any Copilot Studio usage
Both policies keep billing the same usage independently, so the customer pays twice until the Power Platform policy is deleted
The environment is blocked until one of the two policies has been deleted
questions.explanation: Copilot Studio in Microsoft 365 Cost Management is opt-in. Until a resource-based policy covers an environment or agent, Power Platform admin center controls stay in effect. Once covered, the Microsoft 365 policy takes precedence (Microsoft 365 before Power Platform, then resource-based before identity-based). Removing the policy restores the Power Platform setup. AI Builder isn't covered.

questions.question: What does the Microsoft 365 Copilot Cost Management API report usage in?
choices: Azure Cost Management line items, with resource tags
Raw tokens per model, per user and per agent
Credits only, without currency costs, invoices or forecasts
US dollars, at the customer's negotiated effective rate
questions.explanation: Microsoft says the API reports usage in AI credits and doesn't include pricing, invoices, currency costs or purchasing forecasts. FinOps teams must apply their own effective rate (PAYG, pack or P3) to get dollars, and reconcile with Azure invoices.

questions.question: Once usage-based billing is activated with the default spending policy, what happens when prepaid credits run out?
choices: Usage continues on pay-as-you-go through the preconfigured default billing method
Microsoft emails a quote that a billing admin must approve before usage resumes
The tenant is moved onto a P3 pre-purchase plan automatically at the 5% tier
All metered services stop for everyone until the next calendar month begins
questions.explanation: Microsoft's setup page says a default billing method is preconfigured and usage automatically continues on a pay-as-you-go basis when prepaid credits are used up. If the customer wants a hard ceiling, they need limited budgets on their policies.

questions.question: What are Microsoft's rough planning estimates for Copilot Cowork credit consumption per task?
choices: Light 1–3, medium 3–7, heavy over 7 credits per task
Light 100–300, medium 300–700, heavy over 700 credits per task
10,000 credits per user per month, billed whether used or not
A flat 12 credits per task regardless of size
questions.explanation: Microsoft's Copilot Credits guidance gives rough Cowork estimates: light 100–300, medium 300–700, heavy 700+ credits per task, about $1 to $7+ each at PAYG list. Building apps in Cowork is higher (roughly 250 to 1,350+). Cost depends on four buckets: models, runtime, context and tools.

questions.question: A customer licenses 2,000 users for Copilot and expects each to run five medium Cowork tasks per week. Using Microsoft's 300–700 credit medium estimate, what's the rough monthly PAYG exposure?
choices: About $120,000–$280,000 per month in credits, on top of the $60,000 in seats
About $12–$28 million per month in credits, on top of the seats
Nothing beyond the $60,000 in seats, because Cowork tasks are part of the 'everyday AI' included in the Copilot license
About $1,200–$2,800 per month in credits, on top of the seats
questions.explanation: 2,000 users × 5 tasks × ~4 weeks = 40,000 tasks a month. At 300–700 credits each that's 12M–28M credits, or $120K–$280K at $0.01. Plus 2,000 × $30 = $60K in seats. Agentic work can cost more than the seats, so model usage scenarios, not seat counts.

questions.question: Which Cowork activities count toward the organization's Copilot Credit consumption?
choices: Model responses, tool and skill calls, image generation and browser tasks
Only the final deliverable Cowork produces is billed; planning, reasoning, tool calls and browser steps along the way are free
Only the final document or deliverable that Cowork produces
Nothing, as long as the user started the task from Teams
questions.explanation: Microsoft's Cowork governance page lists model responses, tool and skill calls, image generation and browser tasks as counting toward consumption. Long multi-step tasks with many tool calls add up, and plugin tool calls (a Genie plugin, for example) contribute too.

questions.question: Besides usage, what recurring charge does Microsoft's guidance list for an Autopilot agent account?
choices: Nothing. Only task usage is billed
100 Copilot Credits per agent per month
$30 per agent per month, like a user license
1,000 Copilot Credits per user per month
questions.explanation: Microsoft's guidance lists a recurring charge of 100 Copilot Credits per agent per month for an Autopilot agent account, plus usage-based activity. Persistent agents have a standing cost even when idle, so lifecycle management (retiring unused agents) is a cost control, not just hygiene.

questions.question: What is the Copilot Credit Pre-Purchase Plan (P3)?
choices: A free credit grant that Microsoft gives new Microsoft 365 Copilot customers
A monthly add-on to the Microsoft 365 Copilot seat that includes a fixed bundle of credits per user, billed with the license
A three-year reserved instance for Copilot Studio environments and storage
A one-year, pay-upfront pool of Copilot Credit Commit Units with tiered discounts off PAYG
questions.explanation: P3 is a one-year, pay-upfront purchase of Copilot Credit Commit Units (CCCUs) applied to eligible Copilot Credit usage. Discounts run from 5% (300,000 credits) to 20% (300,000,000 credits). It's bought in the Azure portal under Reservations and needs a billing policy tied to an Azure subscription.

questions.question: What discount does the largest P3 tier (300,000,000 credits) carry, and what does the smallest tier (300,000) carry?
choices: 20% at the top tier and 5% at the smallest
35% at the top tier and 0% at the smallest
15% at every tier
50% at the top tier and 10% at the smallest
questions.explanation: Microsoft's nine P3 tiers: 300K (5%), 1.5M (6%), 3M (7%), 15M (8%), 30M (10%), 75M (12%), 150M (14%), 225M (17%), 300M (20%). Microsoft's own example: 1.5M credits is $15,000 at PAYG and $14,100 at the 6% tier.

questions.question: A customer over-buys a P3 plan and wants to cancel or exchange it mid-term. What does Microsoft's documentation say?
choices: It can be cancelled within 30 days for a prorated refund of unused credits
No. Purchases are final, and unused credits expire at the end of the term
It can be exchanged for Azure reserved instances of equal remaining value
Yes, and unused credits roll into the next year's plan automatically
questions.explanation: P3 cancel and exchange operations aren't supported and all purchases are final. Plans can't be split or merged, though scope and ownership can change. Unused credits expire at term end, P3 auto-renews by default, and P3 discounts don't combine with other discounts. Size it on observed usage, not projections.

questions.question: What changes for Copilot Credit P3 purchases starting January 1, 2027?
choices: P3 is sold and renewed only through EA or CSP; MCA-E customers move to AI Flex
P3 moves to the Microsoft 365 admin center, and its discounts double for anything purchased or renewed after that date
P3 is retired, and all customers move to monthly capacity packs
P3 can only be bought in the Microsoft 365 admin center, not in Azure
questions.explanation: From January 1, 2027, P3 can be bought or renewed only through an EA or CSP. Online purchase and the built-in tiered discounts end for other channels, and MCA-E customers can't buy or renew P3. For an MCA-E customer planning a commitment, the purchase channel and timing matter now.

questions.question: What does Microsoft's AI Flex Plan let a customer do?
choices: Fund Copilot Credits plus Foundry, GitHub AI and Security Copilot from one commitment
Swap Microsoft 365 Copilot seats between users every month and convert unused seats into Copilot Credits at list price
Reassign Microsoft 365 Copilot seats between users every month at no cost
Buy Copilot seats on a monthly term without the usual monthly-billing premium
questions.explanation: Microsoft's credits guidance describes the AI Flex Plan as a one- or three-year commitment, paid upfront or monthly through MCA-E, funding Copilot Credits along with Microsoft Foundry, GitHub AI and Security Copilot. It's Microsoft's way to pool AI spend across products, which raises the switching cost of choosing a non-Microsoft agent platform later.

questions.question: At what level are Copilot Credits pooled?
choices: Per Azure subscription only
Per agent, with no sharing
Per user, matching the Copilot license
At the tenant level
questions.explanation: Microsoft: 'Copilot Credits are pooled at the tenant level.' Admins can allocate capacity to Power Platform environments and set limits per agent, user or group. Without allocation, one runaway agent can drain capacity for everyone.

questions.question: Which tool does Microsoft provide to estimate Copilot Studio agent costs before building?
choices: The Power BI Premium capacity estimator
The Copilot Studio agent usage estimator
The Azure Pricing Calculator for Bot Service
Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager
questions.explanation: Microsoft publishes the Copilot Studio agent usage estimator, plus Copilot Credit Estimators for Cowork, the Copilot harness, and Copilot Studio, Dynamics 365 and Microsoft 365 agents. Microsoft says estimators don't guarantee final costs. Validate with a metered pilot.

questions.question: What did Copilot Studio 'messages' become on September 1, 2025?
choices: Azure OpenAI tokens, billed per 1,000 tokens
Agent Units, at double the previous per-unit price and with a new monthly minimum
Copilot Credits, with no change in pack quantity or PAYG rate
Power Platform requests, pooled with Power Apps
questions.explanation: Microsoft renamed messages to Copilot Credits on September 1, 2025, with no change in quantity per prepaid pack or the PAYG rate. Older blogs and analyst notes still say 'messages', and some show outdated rates (for example 30 for tenant graph grounding instead of 10).

questions.sectionName: Building and governing Copilot Studio agents
questions.question: Where do admins configure data policies (DLP) that govern Copilot Studio agents?
choices: In Microsoft Entra admin center under Conditional Access
In the Microsoft Purview portal
In the Power Platform admin center
In each agent's settings in Copilot Studio
questions.explanation: Copilot Studio agents are governed by Power Platform data policies, configured in the Power Platform admin center by tenant or environment admins. Policies can apply to all environments (including new ones), selected environments, or all except some.

questions.sectionName: Building and governing Copilot Studio agents
questions.question: Are Power Platform data policies enforced for Copilot Studio agents in every tenant today?
choices: No. Data policies apply only to Power Apps and Power Automate; Copilot Studio agents are governed separately in Microsoft Purview
Only for agents that are published to external channels such as websites
Yes. Since early 2025 enforcement is on for all tenants, and the agent exemption is no longer supported
No. Admins must opt each agent into data policy enforcement individually
questions.explanation: Microsoft says data policy enforcement has been in effect for all tenants since early 2025, and the earlier agent enforcement exemption is no longer supported. Enforcement is real time: makers see disabled connectors or channels, and publishing fails with an error banner.

questions.sectionName: Building and governing Copilot Studio agents
questions.question: Which data policy connector should an admin block to stop makers publishing agents that anyone with the link can use without signing in?
choices: 'Direct Line channels in Copilot Studio', which covers every channel that doesn't require sign-in
'HTTP'
'Skills with Copilot Studio'
'Chat without Microsoft Entra ID authentication in Copilot Studio'
questions.explanation: Blocking 'Chat without Microsoft Entra ID authentication in Copilot Studio' prevents no-authentication agents. It's one of the most important guardrails, because a no-auth agent grounded on internal content is a data-exfiltration path.

questions.sectionName: Building and governing Copilot Studio agents
questions.question: An admin blocks a Power Platform connector in a data policy. What happens to Copilot Studio MCP server tools that rely on that connector?
choices: They switch to the HTTP connector automatically
They work only for licensed Copilot users
They're blocked too
They keep working, because MCP is outside data policy scope
questions.explanation: Microsoft notes that blocking Power Platform connectors also blocks MCP server tools that depend on them. That includes the Azure Databricks connector behind the Genie tool. If a customer's DLP puts Azure Databricks in the Blocked group, the Copilot Studio-to-Genie path won't work.

questions.sectionName: Building and governing Copilot Studio agents
questions.question: Which data policy groups does Power Platform use to classify connectors, and what is the key constraint between them?
choices: Premium, Standard and Custom, based on each connector's licensing tier
Allowed and Denied only; Power Platform doesn't group connectors any further
Business, Non-business and Blocked; one agent can't mix Business and Non-business
Public, Internal and Confidential, mapped from Purview sensitivity labels; agents may only combine connectors of equal rank
questions.explanation: Data policies sort connectors into Business, Non-business and Blocked. An agent can't combine connectors from Business and Non-business. Connectors introduced after 2019 often land in Non-business by default, so a new connector (such as Azure Databricks) may need reclassifying to Business before a Genie agent can use it with SharePoint or Dataverse.

questions.sectionName: Building and governing Copilot Studio agents
questions.question: A customer wants agents to call only approved HTTP endpoints rather than blocking HTTP entirely. What does Copilot Studio support?
choices: A per-agent allow list in Microsoft Purview
Endpoint filtering on the HTTP connector
Restricted Content Discovery for URLs
Nothing. HTTP is all or nothing
questions.explanation: Data policies support endpoint filtering for the HTTP connector, and for knowledge sources like SharePoint and public websites through connector endpoints. Allow-listing endpoints gives makers flexibility while keeping control.

questions.sectionName: Building and governing Copilot Studio agents
questions.question: If a data policy leaves no channel allowed for Copilot Studio, what happens?
choices: Agents can't be published
Agents publish to Teams only
Agents publish but can't be shared
Agents publish to Direct Line only
questions.explanation: Channels are governed as connectors (Teams + Microsoft 365, Direct Line, SharePoint, Facebook, WhatsApp, Omnichannel and more). Direct Line channels are allowed by default. If no channel is allowed, agents can't be published, which some admins use as a deliberate 'build but don't ship' stage.

questions.sectionName: Building and governing Copilot Studio agents
questions.question: Which data policy connector controls whether Copilot Studio agents can use event triggers and automated evaluations with authenticated accounts?
choices: 'Application Insights in Copilot Studio'
'Microsoft Copilot Studio'
'Chat without Microsoft Entra ID authentication in Copilot Studio'
'Omnichannel in Copilot Studio'
questions.explanation: The 'Microsoft Copilot Studio' connector in data policies governs event triggers and automated evaluations using authenticated accounts. Blocking it is a blunt but effective way to stop autonomous agents, which are also the agents the licensed-user exemption doesn't cover.

questions.sectionName: Building and governing Copilot Studio agents
questions.question: What is the default authentication option for new Copilot Studio agents?
choices: No authentication
